findings.title: Array-valued iss bypasses allowedIss via loose .some() match
findings.evidence: The decoder (src/decoder.js) parses the JWT payload with JSON.parse, so an attacker can supply the iss claim as an array of strings. In verifyToken (src/verifier.js:209-227) the claim value is wrapped as `arrayValue = Array.isArray(value)` and `values = arrayValue ? value : [value]`. For the allowedIss validator (created at src/verifier.js:474-476) the `array` flag is unset, but validateClaimType (src/verifier.js:144-151) only checks that each element's typeof is 'string'; it never rejects an array when arrays are not permitted. Execution then reaches the sink at src/verifier.js:159: `if (!values.some(v => allowed.some(a => a.test(v))))`. Because it uses `.some()` over the claim values, a token whose payload is `{"iss":["trusted-issuer","evil-issuer"]}` is accepted by a verifier configured with `allowedIss: 'trusted-issuer'` even though `iss` must be a single StringOrURI (RFC 7519 section 4.1.1) and contains the attacker-controlled issuer 'evil-issuer'. A valid signature is required, so the flaw is an authentication/spoofing bypass of the issuer pin (CWE-290): any token signed by the shared key that carries the trusted issuer anywhere in an array-valued iss is accepted, and downstream code that selects a different array element (e.g. the first) sees an untrusted issuer. The invariant enforced by the reference fix is that scalar claims must satisfy every value, not just one; i.e. non-array validators should use `values.every(...)` and only the array-enabled aud validator should use `.some()`.
